case_name: Prem Prakash v Union of India and Others
facts: The petitioners, Prem Prakash and Dal Chand Anand, are members of a scheduled caste.

On September 26, 1979, the Registrar of the Delhi High Court published a newspaper advertisement that the Delhi High Court will hold an examination for recruitment of officers to the Delhi Judicial Service on January 11, 12 and 13, 1980 in the time scale pay of Rs. 650-1200.

A competitive examination was held in pursuance of the said advertisement in accordance with the Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1970 which were framed by the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in consultation with the High Court of Delhi.
The petitioners appeared for the examination and passed it, though by relaxation of the minimum standard prescribed for passing the examination.
They were then asked to appear at the viva voce test conducted by the Selection Committee, which they did.
Since, only seven open candidates and four Scheduled Caste candidates qualified in these tests, the High Court prepared a merit list of 11 candidates as against 16 vacancies which were advertised.
Dal Chand Anand, who is petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2962 of 1981, was 10th in the merit list while Prem Prakash, who is petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4480 of 1980, was 11th in that list.
They were respectively 3rd and 4th in the merit list amongst the 4 Scheduled Caste Candidates.
Since they did not figure in the final list of candidates selected by the Administrator, they have filed these petitions to challenge their exclusion and non-appointment.
issues: What is the correct interpretation of Rule 28 of the Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1970?
Is the reservation policy for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes applicable to the initial recruitment to the Service or only to subsequent recruitments through competitive examination?
Can the respondents be directed to appoint the petitioners against the vacancies reserved for members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Delhi Judicial Service?
petitioner_arguments: The petitioners argue that they are entitled to appointment against the vacancies reserved for members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Delhi Judicial Service.
They contend that the respondents have failed to comply with the reservation policy for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
They argue that the petitioners have passed the examination and appeared at the viva voce test, but were excluded from the final list of candidates selected by the Administrator.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argue that Rule 28 of the Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1970 only applies to recruitments made through competitive examination.
They contend that the initial recruitment to the Service was not by competitive examination and therefore no reservations were made in favour of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
They argue that the petitioners have failed to demonstrate any prejudice or discrimination against them.
court_reasoning: The Court notes that Rule 28 of the Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1970 provides for special representation for members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in recruitments made through competitive examination.
It observes that the initial recruitment to the Service was not by competitive examination and therefore no reservations were made in favour of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The Court finds that the respondents have failed to comply with the reservation policy for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
It concludes that the petitioners are entitled to appointment against the vacancies reserved for members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Delhi Judicial Service.
holding: The Court directs the respondents to appoint the petitioners against the vacancies reserved for members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Delhi Judicial Service.
It orders that the petitioners be appointed as per the merit list prepared by the High Court.
cases_cited: Prem Prakash v Union of India
